exampleAnswers.title: Completing the Square When the Leading Coefficient Is Negative One

question.explanation:
We begin by completing the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

\[ x^2 +4x -12 \]

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

\[ x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{2}}x -{\color{purple}{12}} \]

Then, we add and then subtract ${\color{blue}{2}}^2,$ writing the constant term ${\color{purple}{12}}$ last:

\[ \underbrace{x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{2}}x + {\color{blue}{2}}^2} - {\color{blue}{2}}^2 - {\color{purple}{12}} \]

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

\[ (x+ {\color{blue}{2}})^2 - {\color{blue}{2}}^2 - {\color{purple}{12}} \]

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

\[ (x+ {\color{blue}{2}})^2 -16. \]

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

\begin{align*} -\left( x^2 +4x -12\right) &= - \left( \left( x+2\right)^2 -16\right) \\[5pt] &= - \left( x+2\right)^2 +16 \\[5pt] &= 16-(x +2)^2. \end{align*}

question.explanation:
We begin by completing the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

\[ x^2 -12x +35 \]

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

\[ x^2 - {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{6}}x +{\color{purple}{35}} \]

Then, we add and then subtract ${\color{blue}{6}}^2,$ writing the constant term ${\color{purple}{35}}$ last:

\[ \underbrace{x^2 - {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{6}}x + {\color{blue}{6}}^2} - {\color{blue}{6}}^2 +{\color{purple}{35}} \]

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

\[ (x- {\color{blue}{6}})^2 - {\color{blue}{6}}^2 + {\color{purple}{35}} \]

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

\[ (x-{\color{blue}{6}})^2 -1. \]

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

\begin{align*} -\left( x^2 -12x +35\right) &= - \left( \left( x-6\right)^2 -1\right) \\[5pt] &= - \left( x-6\right)^2 +1 \\[5pt] &= 1-(x -6)^2. \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Notice that the leading coefficient is $-1.$ So, we take out a factor of $-1$ from the entire expression: \[ -(a^2 +10a - 16) \]

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

\[ a^2 +10a - {\color{purple}{16}} \]

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

\[ a^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{5}}a - {\color{purple}{16}} \]

Then, we add and then subtract ${\color{blue}{5}}^2,$ writing the constant term ${\color{purple}{16}}$ last:

\[ \underbrace{a^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{5}}a + {\color{blue}{5}}^2} - {\color{blue}{5}}^2- {\color{purple}{16}} \]

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

\[ (a+{\color{blue}{5}})^2 - {\color{blue}{5}}^2- {\color{purple}{16}} \]

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

\[ (a+{\color{blue}{5}})^2 - 41 \]

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

\begin{align*} 16-10a-a^2 &= - \left((a+{\color{blue}{5}})^2 - 41\right) \\[5pt] &=-(a +5)^2 +41 \\[5pt] &=41 -(a +5)^2 \end{align*}

\[ x^2 +7x+10 \]

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

\[ x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{\dfrac72}}x +{\color{purple}{10}} \]

Then, we add and then subtract $\left({\color{blue}{\dfrac72}}\right)^2,$ writing the constant term ${\color{purple}{10}}$ last:

\[ \underbrace{x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{\dfrac72}}x + \left({\color{blue}{\dfrac72}}\right)^2} -\left({\color{blue}{\dfrac72}}\right)^2+ {\color{purple}{10}} \]

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

\[ \left(x+ {\color{blue}{\dfrac72}}\right)^2 -\left({\color{blue}{\dfrac72}}\right)^2 + {\color{purple}{10}} \]

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

\[ \left(x+ {\color{blue}{\dfrac72}}\right)^2 -\dfrac94. \]

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

\begin{align*} -\left( x^2 +7x +10\right) &= - \left(\left(x+ \dfrac72\right)^2 -\dfrac94\right) \\[5pt] &= -\left(x+\dfrac72\right)^2 +\dfrac94 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac94-\left(x+ \dfrac72\right)^2. \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Notice that the leading coefficient is $6.$ So, we take out a factor of $6$ from the entire expression:

\[ 6\left(x^2 - \dfrac{1}{3}x\right) \]

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

\[ x^2 - \dfrac{1}{3}x \]

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

\[ x^2-{\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{6}}x \]

Then, we add and then subtract $\left({\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{6}}\right)^2\mathbin{:}$ \[ \underbrace{x^2-{\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{6}}x + \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{6}}\right)^2} - \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{6}}\right)^2 \]

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

\[ \left(x- \dfrac{1}{6}\right)^2 - \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{6}}\right)^2 \] Evaluating the last term, we get

\[ \left(x- \dfrac{1}{6}\right)^2 -\dfrac{1}{36} \]

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression: \begin{align*} 6\left(x^2 - \dfrac{1}{3}x\right) &= 6\left(\left(x- \dfrac{1}{6}\right)^2 -\dfrac{1}{36}\right) \\[5pt] &= 6\left(x- \dfrac{1}{6}\right)^2- 6 \cdot \dfrac{1}{36}\\[5pt] &= 6\left(x- \dfrac{1}{6}\right)^2 - \dfrac{1}{6} \end{align*}

\[ 6\left(x^2+\dfrac{5}{3}x-\dfrac{11}{36}\right) \]

\[ x^2+\dfrac{5}{3} x - {\color{purple}\dfrac{11}{36}} \]

\[ x^2+ {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue} \dfrac{5}{6}}\cdot x - {\color{purple}\dfrac{11}{36}} \]

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

\[ \left(x + \dfrac{5}{6}\right)^2 -\left({\color{blue} \dfrac{5}{6}}\right)^2- {\color{purple}\dfrac{11}{36}} \]

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

\[ \left(x + \dfrac{5}{6}\right)^2 - 1 . \]

question.explanation:
Notice that the leading coefficient is $10.$ So, we take out a factor of $10$ from the entire expression: \[ 10\left(x^2 + \dfrac{2}{10}x + \dfrac{7}{100}\right) \]

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses: \[ x^2 + \dfrac{2}{10}x + {\color{purple}\dfrac{7}{100}} \]

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor: \[ x^2 + {\color{red}{2}} \cdot {\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{10}}x + {\color{purple}\dfrac{7}{100}} \]

Then, we add and then subtract $\left({\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{10}}\right)^2,$ writing the constant term ${\color{purple}\dfrac{7}{100}}$ last: \[ \underbrace{x^2 + {\color{red}{2}} \cdot {\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{10}}x + \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{10}}\right)^2 } - \, \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{10}}\right)^2 + {\color{purple}\dfrac{7}{100}} \]

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows: \[ \left(x + \dfrac{1}{10}\right)^2 - \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{10}}\right)^2 + {\color{purple}\dfrac{7}{100}} \]

Evaluating the last two terms, we get \[ \left(x + \dfrac{1}{10}\right)^2 + \dfrac{3}{50}. \]

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression: \begin{align*} 10\left(x^2 + \dfrac{2}{10}x + \dfrac{7}{100}\right) & = 10\left( \left(x + \dfrac{1}{10}\right)^2 + \dfrac{3}{50}\right)\\[5pt] & = 10\left(x + \dfrac{1}{10}\right)^2 + 10 \cdot \dfrac{3}{50}\\[5pt] & = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{10}\left(x + \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{10}}\right)^2 + \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{3}{5}} \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Notice that the leading coefficient is $-4.$ So, we take out a factor of $-4$ from the entire expression:

\[ -4\left(x^2 - 2x\right) \]

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

\[ x^2 - 2x \]

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

\[ x^2-{\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}1}x \]

Then, we add and then subtract ${\color{blue}1}^2\mathbin{:}$ \[ \underbrace{x^2-{\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}1}x + {\color{blue}1}^2} - {\color{blue}1}^2 \]

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

\[ \left(x - 1\right)^2 - {\color{blue}1}^2 \] Evaluating the last term, we get

\[ \left(x - 1\right)^2 - 1 \]

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression: \begin{align*} -4\left(x^2 - 2x\right) &= -4\left(\left(x- 1\right)^2 -1\right) \\[5pt] &= -4\left(x- 1\right)^2 + (-4) \cdot(-1)\\[5pt] &= -4\left(x- 1\right)^2 + 4 \end{align*}

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

\[ x^2+{\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}4}x+ {\color{purple}12} \]

Then, we add and then subtract ${\color{blue}4}^2,$ writing the constant term ${\color{purple}12}$ last: \[ \underbrace{x^2+{\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}4}x + {\color{blue}4}^2} - {\color{blue}4}^2+ {\color{purple}12} \]

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

\[ (x+4)^2 - {\color{blue}4}^2+ {\color{purple}12} \] Evaluating the last two terms, we get

\[ (x+4)^2 - 4 \]

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression: \begin{align*} -5\left(x^2 + 8x + 12\right) &= -5\left((x+4)^2 - 4\right) \\[5pt] &= -5\left(x+4\right)^2 + (-5)\cdot (-4)\\[5pt] &= -5\left(x+4\right)^2 + 20 \end{align*}

example.title: Completing the Square on an Expression With a Negative Leading Coefficient

question.explanation:
Notice that the leading coefficient is $-2.$ So, we take out a factor of $-2$ from the entire expression:

\[ -2\left(x^2 + 3x\right) \]

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

\[ x^2 + 3x \]

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

\[ x^2+{\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}\dfrac{3}{2}}x \]

Then, we add and then subtract $\left({\color{blue}\dfrac{3}{2}}\right)^2\mathbin{:}$ \[ \underbrace{x^2+{\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}\dfrac{3}{2}}x + \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{3}{2}}\right)^2} - \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{3}{2}}\right)^2 \]

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

\[ \left(x+ \dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2 - \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{3}{2}}\right)^2 \] Evaluating the last term, we get

\[ \left(x+ \dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2 -\dfrac{9}{4} \]

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression: \begin{align*} -2\left(x^2 + 3x\right) &= -2\left(\left(x + \dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2 - \dfrac{9}{4}\right) \\[5pt] &= -2\left(x + \dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2 +(-2)\cdot \left(-\dfrac{9}{4}\right)\\[5pt] &= -2\left(x + \dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2 + \dfrac{9}{2} \end{align*}

example.title: Completing the Square on an Expression With a Negative Leading Coefficient

question.explanation:
Notice that the leading coefficient is $-3.$ So, we take out a factor of $-3$ from the entire expression:

\[ -3\left(y^2-2y-\dfrac{1}{3}\right) \]

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

\[ y^2-2y-{\color{purple} \dfrac{1}{3}} \]

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

\[ y^2-{\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{1}}y-{\color{purple}\dfrac{1}{3} } \]

Then, we add and then subtract ${\color{blue}{1}}^2,$ writing the constant term ${\color{purple}{\dfrac{1}{3}}}$ last:

\[ \underbrace{y^2-{\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{1}}y + {\color{blue}{1}}^2} - {\color{blue}{1}}^2-{\color{purple}\dfrac{1}{3}} \]

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

\[ (y-1)^2 - {\color{blue}{1}}^2-{\color{purple}\dfrac{1}{3}} \]

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

\[ (y-1)^2 - \dfrac{4}{3}. \]

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

\begin{align*} -3\left(y^2-2y-\dfrac{1}{3}\right) &= -3\left(\left(y- 1\right)^2 - \dfrac{4}{3}\right)\\[5pt] &=-3\left(y- 1\right)^2+(-3)\cdot \left(- \dfrac{4}{3}\right)\\[5pt] &=-3\left(y- 1\right)^2+4 \end{align*}
